title: Job, a good man (Job 1–2)
hook: a good man loses everything, and still does not curse God
carry: the lord gave, the lord took

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five books of the Psalms. Your line: every feeling has a psalm. Today, the hardest book of wisdom.

"There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." It opens like a folk tale: once upon a time, far away. Nobody knows for sure where Uz was, and the book never says Job was an Israelite. He's just a man, somewhere east, with seven sons, three daughters, thousands of sheep and camels, and a habit of getting up early to offer sacrifices in case his children had sinned at their parties. Then, in a single day, four messengers arrive. Raiders took the oxen. Fire fell on the sheep. Raiders took the camels. And the last: a great wind hit the house where his children were eating, and they are all dead.
screen: `A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.` → `FOUR MESSENGERS, ONE DAY.` → `EVERYTHING GONE.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible calls Job "perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." Perfect here means whole, blameless, not flawless. First, the reader sees what Job never does: a scene in heaven. The heavenly beings come before God, and among them is one called, in Hebrew, ha-satan. The satan, with the word the in front, more a job title than a name: the adversary, the accuser. Christian tradition has identified him with the devil; some scholars read him here as a member of the heavenly court whose role is to accuse. God points out Job, and the accuser asks the question the whole book turns on: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Is anyone good for free, or only for the reward? Take it all away, and see. So it is taken. Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground and worships: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Then his own body is struck with sores, and he sits in ashes, scraping himself with broken pottery. His wife, who has also just lost ten children, says: curse God, and die. Job answers: "shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" The reader knows about the heavenly scene; Job never finds out. He lives through all of it without the explanation.
screen: `PERFECT: WHOLE, BLAMELESS` · `HA-SATAN: THE ACCUSER` · `DOTH JOB FEAR GOD FOR NOUGHT?` · `JOB NEVER SEES THE REASON` · then, large: `THE LORD GAVE, AND THE LORD HATH TAKEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose trouble makes no sense, a sick child, a friend whose life fell apart through no fault of their own, and don't try to explain it; Job's story begins by refusing to. If you pray, name them before God and leave the why unanswered; if not, wish them strength, like a hand on a shoulder.
Job. A good man from the land of Uz who loses everything, and whose book asks whether anyone loves God for nothing.
Your line: the Lord gave, the Lord took. Job says it in the ashes, not after the ending. Go gently.

howItsDone: Christians often read the book of Job in times of grief and suffering, and Job's words "the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away" are said at many Christian funerals.

fork.setup: in one day you've lost your herds, your servants and all ten of your children. what do you do?
options: tear your robe, fall to the ground, and worship.
demand that God explain himself, right now.
fork.reveal: Job grieves with his whole body and still blesses God's name. the demands for an answer come later, and the book keeps those too.

chat.says: If Job was such a good man, why did all that happen to him?
options: The reader sees a test in heaven; Job never does. He suffers with no reason given.
Job saw the scene in heaven, so he knew all along it was only a test.
He had stopped offering sacrifices, so the accuser was allowed to strike him.
chat.meaning: Before the disasters, the reader sees a scene in heaven. Job never finds out; he lives through it all without the explanation.

notes: Index carry 'the lord gave, the lord took' kept exactly (lowercase); spoken as 'the Lord gave, the Lord took'.
'Perfect' (Hebrew tam) glossed as whole, blameless. Confirm.
Ha-satan: script says Christians have long identified him with the devil, and many scholars read him as a member of the heavenly court in the accuser's role. Confirm this is fair to both readings.
Job's wife: 'curse God, and die' (2:9) paraphrased without quotation marks; the script notes she has also lost ten children, to avoid casting her as a villain.
Location of Uz is debated (Edom and the Hauran are both proposed); softened to 'nobody knows for sure'.
Job 1:21 is widely used in Christian funeral rites (e.g. BCP 1662 Burial of the Dead opening sentences). Confirm for howItsDone.
